title: Second thoughts? Maryland regulators put controversial gas line policy on hold
summary: The Maryland Public Service Commission is delaying a policy that would make new gas customers pay the full cost of pipeline extensions to their properties, a proposal that had enraged natural gas companies. The pause concerns climate advocates.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters May 16, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters May 16, 2026

The Maryland Public Service Commission is delaying a policy that would make new gas customers pay the full cost of pipeline extensions to their properties, a proposal that had enraged natural gas companies.

The about-face on a policy that was set last summer is among the first major decisions by the commission’s new chairman, Kumar Barve, and it caught climate groups and consumer advocates by surprise.

But Barve said he and the other four commissioners felt they needed more information about the policy’s impact on the state’s overall economy and its housing market. Barve, a Democrat who represented Montgomery County in the House of Delegates for more than 30 years, compared it to the fiscal notes lawmakers get on bills.

“In terms of a legislative thing, we always have fiscal notes for bills, and we don’t vote on bills until we have a proper fiscal note,” he said in an interview. “I think this is the equivalent of that.”

The utility regulating commission issued the policy change nearly a year ago under its former chair, who stepped down earlier this year at the urging of Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), who then elevated Barve to the position.

It’s not clear how long the delay will last. But climate groups and consumer advocates, who back the policy change, are frustrated. They expected the May 8 meeting, where the delay was approved, would be a rule-making session, where commissioners would decide on the particulars of how the new rule would be worded.

Moore signs Maryland energy bill aimed at cutting power costs

“It feels like you’re just dragging this on, and wanting it to slowly go away — or get new information in the record for you to point to, to say no,” said Matt Kasper, deputy director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a watchdog group that “exposes the harms posed by fossil-fuel and monopoly utility interests,” according to its website.

The policy’s supporters argue that the costs of continuing to expand Maryland’s natural gas system should no longer be socialized among all ratepayers, especially since the gas system may be phased out one day, as the state aims to turn away from fossil fuels and toward a power grid fueled by clean energy.

Under Maryland law, the state’s carbon emissions must be net-zero by 2045. During his time in the General Assembly, Barve was an architect of that law, the Climate Solutions Now Act of 2022.

“What I’ve heard from other people in the environmental community is that Kumar Barve is a climate champion, so I want to see him bring that energy to the PSC,” said Brittany Baker, who became Maryland director of the Chesapeake Climate Action Network about two years ago.

But the decision to let gas companies keep paying for new lines using their customer base is far from climate-friendly, she said.

“We already know that clean heat is better and cheaper for homes, and so there’s no reason to be getting cold feet,” Baker said.

In its prior order, issued under Commission Chair Fred Hoover in June 2025, the commission was definitive.

“The Commission is persuaded that new natural gas customers should pay the full cost of extending service to them, thus minimizing any future potential for stranded costs with respect to new extensions, and reducing any subsidization of gas extensions,” read the order.

“Obviously something has changed with this commission,” Kasper said. “And I point out, there’s a new chair.”

Sari Amiel, a staff attorney at the Sierra Club, said it would be “unusual and pretty surprising and disappointing” if the commission completely reversed course.

“The commission’s prior orders are persuasive. They’re their own precedent,” she said.

The original order didn’t come in a vacuum, either, she said. Numerous parties commented on the idea under the commission’s docket studying the “Future of Gas” in the state.

Maryland’s Office of People’s Counsel, which represents ratepayers in matters before the commission, has long pushed to end the line-extension policy. The office estimated that changing the policy would save Baltimore Gas & Electric customers $1.05 billion between 2026 and 2035, while Washington Gas customers would save $563 million during that period.

The office’s analysis found that Maryland gas companies have been spending tens of millions of dollars each year to grow the system, and the general customer base pays the price for decades — with interest.

Because they can recover costs through rate increases, the companies offer line extensions to homeowners and businesses for nominal upfront costs, or none at all.

But as more Marylanders decide to switch out old gas furnaces for heat pumps, and leave the gas system, an increasingly small customer base could be stuck with the costs of this expansion, argues Maryland People’s Counsel David Lapp. And he believes low-income Marylanders and tenants will be especially vulnerable, since they may not be able to switch onto electric appliances if the costs of gas increase.

“Sometimes we get characterized as trying to eliminate gas altogether, or stop all gas infrastructure spending. That has not been our position,” Lapp said. “Our position has consistently been that we need to slow down significantly the rate of the spending.”

Lapp said he was “surprised” by the PSC’s decision to pump the brakes, and he feels there is already ample economic evidence in favor of building electrification in Maryland, which has been studied closely by the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.

Moore brings gripes directly to electric grid operator PJM

But the shrinkage of the gas customer base has yet to manifest itself, at least in Baltimore Gas & Electric territory, said Nichole Owens, BGE’s vice president of gas operations.

“The customer gas population has not shrunk,” Owens said.” We look year over year, we’ve seen a steady growth, and that is because customers do have choices.”

“If we have customers that are approaching us about options, because maybe electrification is — it could be too expensive for them, we have a duty of the state to respond to them and to offer service,” Owens said.

BGE, along with Washington Gas and Columbia Gas, applauded the commission’s latest decision.

“We hope that with a thorough, evidence-based review the Commission will recognize that shifting the full upfront cost of gas line connections onto new customers would be a significant policy change with negative impacts on housing costs, customer choice, and energy affordability,” wrote Washington Gas spokesperson David Loewenberg in a statement. “This, at a time when Maryland is short of housing and facing an electricity price crisis.”

During the General Assembly session that adjourned last month, several legislators also expressed concerns about the proposed rule change and housing costs. In fact, the Senate passed a provision that would have overturned the commission’s decision, but that was opposed by the House and ultimately cut from the bill.

The provision came from Sen. Paul Corderman (R-Frederick and Washington), but was embraced by leading Senate Democrats, who allowed it to be added to the sprawling energy bill without debate. Corderman highlighted fears that housing developers looking to extend natural gas to new properties may move to other states if they have to pay the costs of line extensions in Maryland.

“We try to create more housing, and we don’t allow these extensions to exist,” Corderman said last month. “Those housing developments aren’t going to happen.”

Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) said that Democrats accepted Corderman’s amendment because of “genuine concerns about cost.”

“As new housing developments are proposed, if there is not sufficient infrastructure for full electrification, then the energy’s got to come from something,” Ferguson said during an April news conference.
